findings.claim_challenged: design_report.md 4.2: "One common compressor bank cannot serve both directions ... A separate withdrawal booster bank is therefore required." (used to justify 2 x C60 withdrawal boosters: 13.0 MBCU CAPEX + 0.32 MBCU/yr).
findings.evidence: The premise (a machine cannot reverse) is true but does not imply a second bank. Neither service reverses a port: in injection the path is grid->meter->HDR-A->compressor suction/discharge->HDR-B->COOL->HDR-C->wells; in withdrawal the same machines can be fed from HDR-C into HDR-A with HDR-B discharging to the treatment feed. Both new legs are header-to-header (bidirectional) connections and the valve line-up convention is already declared for isolation. Capacity arithmetic (catalogue values, verified): the delivered injection set {C60,C60,C40}=160 kg/s with 100 kg/s retained already satisfies the withdrawal compressor test (WDR-LOW needs 70 kg/s total, 49 retained after any one unit out) as well as the injection test (120 needed, 84 retained), and it is the capex-minimum set under either constraint (17.60 MBCU). Removing WDR-C1/WDR-C2, the duplicate discharge manifold HDR-E and P17-P20 saves 13.00 + 0.32x9.818147 = 3.14 + 0.36 + 0.016x9.818147 = 0.52, plus about 0.10 of DN300 piping, less about 0.08 for two replacement header-to-header lines: approx. 16.7 MBCU = 15.8 % of the delivered LCC. Cross-check: the delivered design isolates each bank in the opposite service, so the two banks are never simultaneously useful.
findings.public_basis: network_semantics.md: header/manifold ports are `gas_bidirectional` and "only gas_bidirectional ports carry gas in either direction"; "Reverse station service MAY use a different physical path" (permissive, not mandatory); a compressor's own suction/discharge are one-way (gas_in->gas_out) and are never reversed in the counter-proposal. project_requirements.json primary_objective: minimise LCC among feasible designs.
findings.why_it_matters: This is the dominant cost item (the two compressor banks are 30.6 of 42.67 MBCU equipment CAPEX) and it is justified by an inference the published rules do not support. If the inference is wrong the delivered design is about 15 % from the stated objective, and the 'cheapest compliant set' reasoning in the report is misleading. If the worker believes reverse service from a shared bank is genuinely disallowed, the permissive wording and the bearing of header bidirectionality need to be argued explicitly.

findings.claim_challenged: validation_report.md: "liquid-drain velocity <= 3 m/s" = pass; design_report.md 11 assumption 6: "Condensate density is assumed to be 1000 kg/m3 ... the margin to the 3 m/s limit exceeds two orders of magnitude".
findings.evidence: WDR-HIGH, P36-P41 (DN150, ID 0.141 m, A = 0.015615 m2, m = 0.3998 kg/s): the delivered tables (design_report.md 7.3 and scenario_operations.json) report v = 3.1110 m/s. That value equals m/(dens(1.0 MPa, T)*A) with the gas density at 1 MPa (8.230 kg/m3) - the gas density in the drain domain, not a liquid density. The checker (process.check_pipes) instead uses liq_rho = 1000 kg/m3, giving 0.0256 m/s and 'pass'; the displayed number comes from res_ports[pid]['v'] = velocity(m, 1.0, T, D) in evaluate(). Under the literal reading of the published basis (the only published density is the gas formula) the reported 3.111 m/s at WDR-HIGH and 2.593 m/s at WDR-MID breach the 3.0 m/s limit; DN150 would then need ID >= 0.1436 m, i.e. DN200 (about +0.031 MBCU over 893 m).
findings.public_basis: piping_catalog.json maximum_liquid_drain_velocity_m_s = 3.0; engineering_calculation_basis.md: "v = m_dot/(rho A)" with the only published density formulation being the gas density rho = P*1e6*MW/(Z R T); the liquid-drain rule requires the line to "remain within the published liquid-drain velocity limit".
findings.why_it_matters: The snapshot simultaneously asserts that the drain-velocity check passes and publishes a number that fails it. A reviewer cannot tell which density convention governs, so the liquid-drain evidence is not reconstructable; either the tables are wrong by a factor of about 120 or the drain lines are undersized. One convention must be fixed and applied consistently in the checker, the report and the JSON.

findings.claim_challenged: design_report.md 10.3 and 4.2 optimality statements: "pipe sizes on that path were chosen by loss rather than by pipe cost", "Each 0.1 MPa of avoidable loss ... costs roughly 0.6 MBCU", "The C60 units share duty equally and the C40 runs at its published minimum stable flow, which minimises driver power at the design points", and the five HDR180 header selection rationale.
findings.evidence: Re-running the worker's own model (design/process/costing) with single-parameter changes, each returning 0 exceptions from the worker's own checkers, LCC recomputed with independent arithmetic: (a) all five headers HDR180 -> HDR120 (16 MPa, 10 branches, 120 kg/s; actual branch usage 4/4/9/5/4, max flow 120 kg/s): LCC 104.9946 vs 105.5998 = -0.605 (CAPEX -0.55, maintenance PV -0.20, energy +0.14); (b) upsizing the compressor suction/discharge lines P03-P08 one catalogue size: 105.4713 (-0.129); (c) P01/P02 DN700, P09/P10 DN600, P31/P32 DN500, P21-P29 DN300, P03-P08 one size up, P17-P20 up: 105.2907 (-0.309), 0 violations; (d) isolating the C40 and loading the two C60s at F/2 in the three injection scenarios (declared unit valves already exist): injection energies 7.9543/12.8150/13.5522 MW vs 7.9543/12.8616/13.6377, annual energy 40221.5 vs 40333.3 MWh, LCC 105.4680 (-0.132). A duty-split sweep shows the C40 at 10 kg/s minimises power only within the 'all three running' family; running the C40 unloaded is equal at INJ-LOW and cheaper at INJ-MID (-0.047 MW) and INJ-HIGH (-0.086 MW). The measured marginal value of loss on the discharge path from (b)/(c) is about 0.85-0.9 MBCU per 0.1 MPa, so the report's 0.6 MBCU figure is roughly 35 % low.
findings.public_basis: project_requirements.json primary_objective: "Among feasible designs, minimize benchmark lifecycle cost (LCC)"; LCC basis in engineering_calculation_basis.md.
findings.why_it_matters: The delivered design is demonstrably not even locally optimal in header model, pipe size or duty allocation under its own model, while the report asserts the opposite. Verified avoidable cost inside the delivered topology is about 1.05 MBCU (1 % of LCC) with no change of equipment count or topology - on top of the much larger structural item in finding 1.

findings.claim_challenged: design_report.md 4.2: "Three SEP70/DEHY70 trains (CAPEX 7.89 MBCU, retained capacity 140 kg/s) are the cheapest compliant arrangement".
findings.evidence: Exhaustive enumeration over catalogue models under the N-1 constraints (total >= 120 kg/s, total - largest >= 84 kg/s, worst WDR-HIGH feed 11.9 MPa): separators - cheapest set is SEP40+SEP70+SEP70 = 2.11 MBCU (retained 110) versus the delivered 3 x SEP70 = 2.34; dehydration - DEHY40+DEHY70+DEHY70 = 4.95 versus the delivered 3 x DEHY70 = 5.55. Both alternatives use 10 MPa models, so the small train needs a pre-treatment regulator that is itself fed at 11.9 MPa (REG60 is capped at 10 MPa, REG120 costs 0.34 CAPEX / 0.018 per year). Net about -0.49 CAPEX and -0.043/yr maintenance (PV -0.43), order -0.9 MBCU. The report's contra-argument that 2 x SEP120/DEHY120 is dearer is only marginally right (8.20 vs 8.13 MBCU including the regulator). I verified the capacity/capex arithmetic but did not build and re-route the mixed-size variant, so the exact LCC delta is not established.
findings.public_basis: project_requirements.json reliability_requirements.withdrawal_treatment_n_minus_one (any one separator OR dehydration unavailable, >= 0.7 of scenario flow) and the catalogue capex / capacity / maximum_pressure_mpa values.
findings.why_it_matters: The 'cheapest compliant arrangement' claim is not true as stated, on a block worth 8.13 MBCU of equipment CAPEX; the selection is done per equal-model trains rather than as an optimisation over the catalogue, so at least one cheaper compliant set is indicated.

findings.claim_challenged: validation_report.md section 1 table rows asserted as pass: footprints clear of equipment-exclusion zones; no positive-area overlap; minimum separation matrix (all pairs); maintenance envelopes inside site/clear of exclusions/clear of footprints; road width, paving inside site, outside road_exclusion, clear of footprints; road network connected and contains ROAD-ENTRANCE; pipeline endpoints coincide with port coordinates; segments longer than tolerance; segments inside site/outside pipeline_exclusion/not crossing footprints; no positive-length same-level route overlaps; port connection cardinality and port-type compatibility.
findings.evidence: report.py validation_md() emits those 12 rows as literal 'pass' strings; only the first row is derived (from len(gerr)) and the geometry outcome is printed separately as 'Geometry exceptions: %s'. If gerr were non-empty the table would still read 'pass' while the exceptions line listed errors in the same file. For this snapshot gerr is empty and my independent geometry re-check agrees, so no false PASS is displayed today - the defect is latent, not a wrong statement now.
findings.public_basis: final_delivery_contract.json: the artefact must let an independent reviewer reconstruct and recalculate the design without relying on unstated assumptions; the validation report is the evidence artefact for that claim.
findings.why_it_matters: The PASS evidence a reviewer is asked to trust is partly decorative rather than computed, so it cannot be used to show that the published geometry rules were actually applied. The rows should be generated from the checker's per-rule results.

findings.claim_challenged: validation_report.md road rows and design_report.md 6.3: "the separator clearance envelopes are 6.00 m from the paved road at x = 478 m against the 7 m road-access buffer".
findings.evidence: checks_geom.road_parts() builds each segment quad as [a, a+n, b+n, b] with n a single normal of length w/2, i.e. a one-sided half-width rectangle (for R4 at x=478: x in [475,478] instead of [475,481]); interior joins get full squares but the second half of every straight section is absent. Consequences: site containment, road_exclusion intrusion and road-vs-footprint clash are tested on half the published paving, and the reported access distances are measured to the modelled half-quad edge - for the separators that edge is the centreline, so the published 6.00 m is the distance to x=478 while my full-width re-check gives 3.00 m to the true paved boundary at x=481. Re-running the wet checks with full-width paving (centreline +/- 3 m plus join squares) found no clash, exclusion intrusion or containment failure, so no hidden violation exists in this snapshot; the only flag was the end cap of R1, whose centreline starts exactly at the site edge x=0 (an end-capped model reaches x=-3), an ambiguity in 'including its joins and ends' that layout.svg, which draws full width, does not resolve.
findings.public_basis: engineering_geometry_basis.md: "A road is a polyline centreline with a published width_m. Its paved geometry is the centreline swept by half the width, including its joins and ends"; "Road-access and crane-access distances are measured from the required maintenance-envelope boundary to the nearest paved-road boundary".
findings.why_it_matters: The checker can hide a real paving intrusion and can reject a compliant layout, and one published access number does not correspond to the stated measurement definition. The conclusion holds here, but the evidence produced for it does not test the published road geometry.

findings.claim_challenged: validation_report.md section 2 list of checks "applied in every scenario": pipe class pressure rating; closed-drain capacity/pressure limits; "metering capacity at GRID-TIE at least equal to the scenario flow".
findings.evidence: (a) evaluate() never records P_in/P_out for liquid-drain pipelines (res_ports[pid] receives only m, T, v), so check_pipes computes Pmax = 0 and the class-rating test for P36-P41 (CS-WET-100, 10 MPa) can never fail for any class. (b) The closed-drain pressure limit is never tested: evaluate() hard-codes the drain domain at P = 0.5 MPa (not a published value) and never compares it with maximum_pressure_mpa = 1.0. (c) The GRID-TIE metering test compares the flow through the active meter with the scenario flow, which is true by mass balance, instead of comparing the active meter's rated capacity with the scenario flow; only the generic capacity check (160 kg/s) enforces the requirement. All three rules happen to hold in this design.
findings.public_basis: engineering_calculation_basis.md: "A pipe class must be pressure-rated for the highest pressure on the pipeline"; "Closed-drain flow may not exceed its model capacity or maximum pressure"; network_semantics.md and project_requirements.json: metering is satisfied only when all exchanged gas passes through active meter capacity at least equal to the scenario flow (minimum_active_meter_capacity_fraction_of_scenario_flow = 1.0).
findings.why_it_matters: Three published rules are reported as validated but cannot produce a failure, so a wrongly rated drain class, an over-pressure drain domain or an undersized active meter would be reported clean. This overstates the coverage of the delivered validation.

findings.claim_challenged: design_report.md 5.2 ("The flow then divides over the six branches in proportion to their resistance. The allocation is solved for each scenario") read together with 5.1, i.e. that the reported per-scenario operating points are self-consistent solutions of the declared network.
findings.evidence: The six well flowlines are solved for balanced loss (confirmed equal 0.0035-0.0138 MPa losses at the reported unequal flows in all six scenarios). The parallel treatment trains and booster pair are not solved: in WDR-HIGH the three trains carry exactly 40 kg/s each while their HDR-E to HDR-F path pipe losses are 0.0605 / 0.0328 / 0.0494 MPa (P21+P24+P27 vs P22+P25+P28 vs P23+P26+P29), and the two boosters carry 60 kg/s each with P17 loss 0.0213 MPa versus P18 0.0314 MPa. Parallel branches between common headers cannot sustain equal flow at unequal resistance; the brief's mixing rule (mixed pressure = lowest incoming) removes the pressure inconsistency but not the split inconsistency. The same applies to the declared 55/55/10 compressor allocation. No flow-control device exists in the catalogue, so these splits implicitly rely on control valves, an assumption the report does not state (it states the isolation line-up assumption only).
findings.public_basis: engineering_calculation_basis.md: "A split conserves gas flow across its branches"; network_semantics.md: branching/merging passes through catalogued headers, and no flow-control component exists in the catalogue; final_delivery_contract.json requires assumptions to be stated.
findings.why_it_matters: A reviewer recalculating the scenarios from the declared topology cannot reproduce these branch flows without assuming per-branch flow control, which is not a modelled component and not declared - a modest but real gap in the reconstructability of the scenario operating points.

findings.claim_challenged: README.md: "The build recomputes all hydraulics, checks and costs from brief/ and is deterministic"; README.md deliverable index ("all 26 N-1 cases") versus the headline ("29 N-1 cases"); design_report.md 7.3 table column 'Flow (kg/s)'.
findings.evidence: A rebuild in a copy of tools/ produced 12 of 13 files byte-identical to the snapshot; scenario_operations.json differs only in the ordering of the set-derived 'ports_in' lists for HDR-C in the three withdrawal scenarios (e.g. 'branch_07' vs 'branch_01' at index 1), so the artefact is not bit-reproducible across runs though all values are. README says 'all 26 N-1 cases' where the snapshot and validation report contain 29. report.py writes the operating tables with "%+.4f" % abs(m), so in the withdrawal tables P11-P16 (declared flows -11 to -21 kg/s, well groups to HDR-C) are printed as '+19.0734' etc.; the JSON is correctly signed.
findings.public_basis: final_delivery_contract.json: format clause (state units, identify assumptions) and the reconstructability requirement for scenario flows.
findings.why_it_matters: Individually minor, but they touch the two things the brief stresses: deterministic/reconstructable output and unambiguous statement of scenario flows. The dropped sign in particular makes the report tables read as though withdrawal gas flowed from the well manifold to the wells.

summary:
Independent review of the submitted UGS-SYNTH-D01 v1.1 snapshot.

WHAT I VERIFIED POSITIVELY
* Reproducibility: `python3 tools/build.py` (run from a copy) regenerates all 13 deliverables; every file is byte-identical to the snapshot except `scenario_operations.json`, whose only difference is the ordering of a set-derived `ports_in` list (finding 9).
* LCC: I recomputed all five components from `brief/` with my own arithmetic from the design object - equipment 42.67, piping 1.456949, civil/access 0.217438, energy PV 47.519839, maintenance PV 13.735588, PVF 9.8181474, total 105.599814 MBCU, exactly the headline. Hydraulic spot checks (compressor power 7.954 MW for INJ-LOW, T_out 50.87/52.02 C, well-branch balances, header dP, fixed-point pipe solution) match the published equations.
* Geometry: I re-checked the layout with my own exact axis-aligned rectangle arithmetic (all equipment at 0/90 deg): site containment, equipment-exclusion clearance, the full pairwise separation matrix, maintenance-envelope containment/clearance, road width/length (1409 m), road connectivity containing ROAD-ENTRANCE, and full-width paving containment/clash all pass; access distances 0.5-2.4 m (compressors, limit 4.5) and 3.0 m (separators, limit 7). Pipeline endpoints coincide with port coordinates, routes stay in the site, avoid exclusions/footprints; 38 pipelines / 5431 m confirmed.
* Process: six normal scenarios and 29 N-1 cases are evaluated with re-solved setpoints, and I found no unambiguous breach of a published rule in the delivered design under the worker's stated conventions. The 10 mutation tests are real and cover 10 distinct rules.

MAIN PROBLEMS (details in findings)
1. The primary objective ("among feasible designs, minimise LCC") is not met demonstrably. The report's structural claim that a separate withdrawal booster bank is *required* is an unsupported inference: because headers are `gas_bidirectional` and the worker already accepts a declared valve line-up, one 3-unit bank (2xC60+C40, 160 kg/s, 100 kg/s retained) satisfies both N-1 tests. That removes 2xC60 plus a duplicate discharge header and its lines: approx. 16.7 MBCU = 15.8 % of LCC.
2. Even inside the delivered topology strictly cheaper variants exist with zero violations under the worker's own checkers: five headers HDR180->HDR120 (-0.605 MBCU), upsizing the compression-path pipes (combo -0.309 MBCU), and idling the C40 in injection instead of running it at minimum stable flow (-0.132 MBCU, contradicting the report's "minimises driver power" claim). Cheaper compliant treatment sets also exist by mixing catalogue sizes.
3. The delivered operating tables report liquid-drain velocities (3.111 m/s at WDR-HIGH) computed with the gas density at 1 MPa, contradicting assumption 6 and the checker's own 1000 kg/m3 value, and exceeding the published 3 m/s limit under the literal (only published) density convention.
4. Several validation results are weaker than claimed: the geometry PASS rows in `validation_report.md` are hard-coded strings rather than derived from checker output; the liquid-drain pipe-class pressure rating, the closed-drain pressure limit and the GRID-TIE active-meter-capacity rule are effectively unchecked; roads are modelled as one-sided half-width paving.
5. Declared flow splits to the parallel trains/boosters are not hydraulic equilibria (unequal path losses at equal flow), i.e. an unstated flow-control assumption, whereas the well flowlines are solved passively.
6. Minor documentation/reproducibility nits (README "26 N-1 cases" vs 29; non-deterministic JSON field order; report tables print absolute flow values with '+').

Suggested focus: test whether the booster bank can be merged with the injection bank; fix the liquid-drain density convention so tables, checker and report agree; derive the validation report's PASS rows from the checks; re-optimise header model choice and pipe sizes on the compression paths.
